title: Hutchinson's Historical Essay Concerning Witchcraft: Scholarly Historical Critique
description: Francis Hutchinson, an Anglican clergyman, published Historical Essay Concerning Witchcraft in 1718, the first systematic historical treatment of witch prosecution as a historical phenomenon requiring explanation rather than theological resolution. Hutchinson assembled historical evidence of miscarriages of justice, demonstrated how confession and accusation patterns were shaped by procedure and social pressure rather than actual witch activity, and argued from historical evidence that the people executed had been innocent. Unlike earlier skeptics who argued from theology or natural philosophy, Hutchinson approached the question as a historian, examining the evidence critically. His work marks an important early moment in the development of the critical history of witchcraft.
historiographical_note: Ian Bostridge's Witchcraft and Its Transformations (1997) positions Hutchinson as a key transitional figure between theological debate about witchcraft and historical scholarship on it. Keith Thomas in Religion and the Decline of Magic acknowledged Hutchinson as a precursor to modern historical approaches. The shift from asking 'are witches real?' to 'how did people come to believe in witches?' that Hutchinson represents is foundational for all subsequent witchcraft historiography.
source_method: Hutchinson, Historical Essay Concerning Witchcraft (1718); Bostridge (1997); secondary scholarship on Enlightenment skepticism
